headline: US and Iran reignite their war over the Strait of Hormuz: Trump drops a 20% shipping fee but presses a naval blockade as strikes fly, pushing oil to a one-month high.
the_big_picture: The single thread running through today is the re-escalation of the US-Iran conflict at the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. Trump backed off a threatened 20% transit fee but is pushing ahead with a naval blockade while both sides trade strikes and tankers come under attack, sending crude to a one-month high. That oil spike is the hinge for everything downstream: US inflation cooled to 3.5% but officials flagged fresh upside risk, India's inflation just breached its central bank's target, the rupee slid past 96 and the Sensex fell. Running underneath, an AI storyline cuts both ways: IBM shed roughly $70bn in a day after stumbling on AI deals, even as China's AI-driven exports jumped 27% and Nvidia began shipping powerful H200 chips into China.

stories.title: China and Philippines clash for a third time in a week at Scarborough Shoal
key_points: China Coast Guard fired water cannon at a Philippine vessel near Scarborough Shoal
Third confrontation between the two countries in five days
Comes as ASEAN foreign ministers meet in Manila; China warned of 'bitter consequences'
Beijing says it showed 'restraint'; Manila disputes that account
stories.background: Scarborough Shoal is a fishing ground in the South China Sea that sits within the Philippines' internationally recognized exclusive economic zone but has been under de facto Chinese control since a 2012 standoff. A 2016 international tribunal ruling rejected China's broader claims to the sea, but Beijing has never accepted it.
stories.what_happened: On July 24-25, China Coast Guard ships repeatedly fired water cannon at Philippine government vessels — including one carrying a CNN crew — that were delivering fuel and food to Filipino fishermen near Scarborough Shoal. The Philippine Coast Guard said a Chinese vessel sprayed the ship BRP Cape San Agustin from close range while being shadowed by at least six Chinese coast guard and militia vessels. It was the third clash in five days, following an earlier incident at Second Thomas Shoal in which Manila said a sailor was struck and injured.
stories.why_it_matters: Scarborough Shoal is one of the most contested flashpoints in the South China Sea, a waterway that carries roughly a third of global shipping trade. Repeated close-quarters confrontations raise the risk of a miscalculation that could pull in the United States, which has a mutual defense treaty with the Philippines.
stories.ripple_effects: The escalation could pressure Washington to reaffirm its defense commitments to Manila, strain China's relations with ASEAN nations meeting in the Philippines this week, and add friction to Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's earlier warning that Manila would face 'bitter consequences' for resisting Beijing.
stories.why_now: This is the latest and third confrontation in a week-long escalation, timed alongside ASEAN's annual foreign ministers' meetings taking place in Manila.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Philippines and the US respond with a formal diplomatic or military signal, and whether further resupply missions in coming days trigger new clashes.

key_terms.definition: A 200-nautical-mile area off a country's coast where international law gives it rights to fish and other resources.
An international arbitration panel decision that found China's expansive South China Sea claims have no legal basis under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, though China has ignored it.

stories.the_lesson: Disputed borders that never escalate into open war can still produce a steady drip of dangerous confrontations for years — diplomatic warnings rarely resolve the underlying territorial contest driving them.
stories.market_link: Repeated clashes near one of the world's busiest shipping lanes add a low-grade but persistent geopolitical risk premium for Asian trade and shipping insurance, though no major market moves have been tied to this incident yet.

stories.title: Zelensky warns of a new 'massive' Russian strike, as Ukraine hits back at a Russian refinery 2,000km from the front
key_points: Zelensky says intel shows Russia has 'readied missiles' for a massive strike within 48 hours
Comes a day after a Russian missile killed 10 at a Ukrainian arms exhibition near Kyiv
Ukraine struck Russia's Tyumen oil refinery deep inside Russian territory in response
Russia says it downed 571 Ukrainian drones overnight
stories.background: Russia has been at war with Ukraine since its 2022 invasion; despite periodic US-brokered diplomatic efforts to end the fighting, both sides continue trading long-range strikes deep behind the front lines. On Friday, July 24, a Russian ballistic missile struck an arms exhibition near Kyiv, killing at least 10 people including senior Ukrainian security officials — one of the deadliest single strikes on Ukrainian soil in months.
stories.what_happened: Following Friday's strike on the Kyiv-area arms exhibition, President Zelensky said Saturday that Ukrainian intelligence indicates Russia has 'readied missiles' for a further 'massive' attack within 48 hours. In response, Ukraine's special forces struck the Tyumen oil refinery deep inside Russia, roughly 2,000km from the front line — a sign Ukraine's long-range strike capability keeps expanding. Russia's defense ministry said it downed 571 Ukrainian drones overnight, and Kyiv region declared July 25 a day of mourning for Friday's strike victims.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchange shows the war escalating rather than winding down even as diplomats discuss peace tracks elsewhere. A further 'massive' Russian strike, if it materializes, would mark one of the most significant escalations of the war in months and test how far Western allies are willing to go in response.
stories.ripple_effects: Ukraine's deep strike on a Russian refinery adds a fresh supply-side risk to global oil markets already jumpy over Middle East tensions; a further Russian strike, if it happens, would likely accelerate calls in Washington and Europe for tougher sanctions and more air-defense support for Ukraine.
stories.why_now: Zelensky's 48-hour warning and Ukraine's refinery strike both landed within the last day, marking a sharp escalation after a period of relative diplomatic focus on reviving talks.
stories.watch_next: Whether Russia carries out the 'massive' attack Zelensky warned of within the next 48 hours, and how the US and NATO respond if it does.

key_terms.definition: A missile that is powered and guided only for the first part of its flight, then falls on a predictable arc toward its target, making it hard to intercept.

stories.the_lesson: Diplomatic tracks and battlefield escalation can run in parallel — a war doesn't pause just because talks are happening somewhere else, and strikes on 'soft' targets like industry events are often deliberate signals, not accidents.
stories.market_link: Ukraine's retaliatory strike on Russia's Tyumen refinery adds a fresh supply-risk headline for oil markets already elevated on Middle East tensions.

thread.previously: A Russian ballistic missile struck an arms exhibition near Kyiv on July 24, killing at least 10 people including senior Ukrainian security officials — one of the deadliest single strikes on Ukrainian soil in months.
thread.changed: Zelensky now warns Russia has 'readied missiles' for a further massive strike within 48 hours, and Ukraine has retaliated by striking a Russian oil refinery 2,000km from the front line.

stories.title: Netanyahu's toughest challenger yet: ex-army chief Eisenkot now polls ahead of Likud
key_points: Gadi Eisenkot's new Yashar party has overtaken Netanyahu's Likud in seat projections
One poll gives Yashar a record 25 seats to Likud's low
Eisenkot leads Netanyahu 46%-40% as preferred PM in another poll
Israel votes October 27 — but the opposition still can't form a majority alone
stories.background: Gadi Eisenkot is a former Israeli military chief of staff who lost his son and two nephews fighting in Gaza. He resigned from Netanyahu's war cabinet in 2024, accusing the prime minister of lacking a strategy in Gaza, and has since built a new centrist party, Yashar ('Straight'), positioning himself as the main alternative to Israel's longest-serving prime minister.
stories.what_happened: A new Times of Israel/Zman poll puts Yashar at a record 25 Knesset seats, four ahead of Likud — up from a 2-seat lead the week before. A separate Maariv poll conducted July 22–23 has Eisenkot leading Netanyahu 46% to 40% on the question of preferred prime minister. Israel's national election is set for October 27.
stories.why_it_matters: Netanyahu has dominated Israeli politics for most of the last two decades. A credible, rising challenger — especially one with military credibility and no history with Netanyahu's governing style — changes the political calculus for how Israel manages the tail end of the Gaza war, the confrontation with Iran, and eventual reconstruction diplomacy.
stories.ripple_effects: Even with a seat lead, Yashar and the broader anti-Netanyahu bloc still can't form a majority without support from Arab parties — a politically fraught step in Israel that could itself become a campaign flashpoint. Investors and allies (the US, Gulf states negotiating over Gaza's future) will increasingly price in the chance of a post-Netanyahu Israel.
stories.why_now: This poll is the highest seat count yet recorded for Yashar, marking a new high-water mark in a months-long trend of Eisenkot closing the gap and then passing Likud — making it a genuine milestone rather than routine noise.
stories.watch_next: Whether Yashar's lead holds through the summer, and whether Eisenkot can assemble a workable coalition math with just over three months until the October 27 vote.

key_terms.definition: Israel's parliament; a party needs enough allied seats there to form a governing coalition.

stories.the_lesson: In parliamentary systems, leading in seat polls isn't the same as being able to govern — coalition arithmetic (who can actually agree to sit together) often matters more than who's in first place.

stories.title: Trump quietly halts nightly US strikes on Iran, breaking a 13-day streak
key_points: US skipped a night of strikes on Iran for the first time in nearly two weeks
Trump personally ordered the pause on Friday, officials say
No new Iranian strikes on US targets were reported either
Houthi attacks on Saudi oil sites kept a separate front open
stories.background: On June 27, a US-brokered ceasefire between Israel/the US and Iran collapsed, and the US began nightly bombing runs on Iranian targets that ran for 13 straight days. At least four US service members and dozens of Iranians have been killed since. Trump had recently floated a 'massive attack' but also said negotiations might make it unnecessary.
stories.what_happened: US Central Command did not announce any new overnight strikes on Iran for the first time since the campaign began nearly two weeks ago. Trump directed the military not to conduct new strikes on Friday, breaking the daily-attack pattern. Iran also reported no new strikes on American targets overnight.
stories.why_it_matters: A pause doesn't mean the war is over — Trump's own team says it's unclear if this is a one-off lull or the start of a real de-escalation. But after 13 straight days of daily bombing, any break in the pattern is the first tangible sign either side may be looking for an exit ramp.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil markets, which have been jumpy on Iran-war risk (Brent above $100), will watch closely for whether the pause holds — a real de-escalation would ease the 'war premium' baked into crude and Gulf shipping insurance. It could also take some heat off Gulf allies like Saudi Arabia, which is simultaneously fending off Houthi missile and drone attacks on its own oil infrastructure.
stories.why_now: The pause comes right after Trump publicly mused that a 'massive attack' on Iran 'may not be necessary' — suggesting the halt reflects a deliberate, if untested, shift in his approach rather than a battlefield lull.
stories.watch_next: Whether the US resumes strikes in the next 24–48 hours, which would confirm this was a one-off rather than a genuine pause.

key_terms.definition: The US military headquarters responsible for operations across the Middle East, including strikes on Iran.

stories.the_lesson: In a war run by daily executive decisions rather than a fixed campaign plan, a single quiet night can be read two ways — the start of de-escalation, or just a pause before the next order. Watch what happens next, not the pause itself.
stories.market_link: Brent crude (already above $100/barrel on Iran-war risk) and oil-tanker insurance rates are the most direct market read — a sustained pause would ease the war-risk premium; a resumption would likely push crude higher again.

thread.previously: We reported Trump was floating that a bigger attack on Iran might not be necessary and was considering negotiations, even as US strikes hit a 13th consecutive night.
thread.changed: That talk turned into action: the US skipped a night of strikes entirely for the first time since the campaign began, and Iran didn't retaliate either — though officials caution it may not last.

stories.title: SpaceX's Starship completes its most successful test yet, deploying 20 next-gen Starlink satellites
key_points: Starship's 13th test flight launched from Texas at 10:51pm UTC Friday
The Super Heavy booster made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf
Starship deployed 20 upgraded 'V3' Starlink satellites — its first real payload
The ship itself splashed down under control in the Indian Ocean as planned
stories.background: Starship is SpaceX's giant, fully-reusable next-generation rocket — the vehicle NASA plans to use to land astronauts on the Moon later this decade, and the one SpaceX eventually wants to send to Mars. Earlier test flights had mixed results, including several that ended in explosions, as SpaceX iterates fast and learns from failures in public view rather than testing quietly for years first.
stories.what_happened: SpaceX launched Starship's 13th test flight from Starbase, Texas, at 10:51pm UTC on July 24. The Super Heavy booster separated about two minutes into flight and made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf. The Starship upper stage carried 20 next-generation 'V3' Starlink satellites — the first time this Starship version carried a real operational payload — deployed them successfully, and then splashed down under control in the Indian Ocean as planned. SpaceX confirmed it made contact with all 20 satellites afterward.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the first time the newest Starship version has successfully delivered and deployed an actual satellite payload, a major milestone toward routine, reusable Starship flights that could sharply cut launch costs and expand Starlink's next-generation broadband network.
stories.ripple_effects: Boosts confidence in NASA's Artemis Moon-landing timeline, which depends on a working Starship; strengthens SpaceX's lead over rivals like Amazon's Kuiper in the satellite-broadband race; and could speed up rollout of Starlink V3's higher-bandwidth, laser-linked service.
stories.why_now: This was the second flight of the upgraded 'V3' Starship design, coming after a less successful first attempt and a launch delay for post-abort engine work.
stories.watch_next: Whether SpaceX attempts to catch the booster back at the launch tower (instead of a splashdown) and deploys a full operational batch of Starlink satellites on the next flight.

key_terms.definition: The giant first-stage rocket that lifts Starship off the pad; SpaceX designs it to be reused, like the booster on its smaller Falcon 9 rockets.

stories.the_lesson: Ambitious engineering programs often move faster by testing in public and learning from visible failures than by trying to get everything right before the first launch — each Starship flight, even the ones that end badly, feeds data back into the next design.
stories.market_link: Positive read-through for SpaceX-linked suppliers and Starlink's competitive position against satellite-internet rivals; SpaceX itself is privately held.

stories.title: Wildfires force over 250,000 evacuations across southwestern France and central Spain
key_points: Bordeaux suburbs ordered to evacuate as the Gironde fire triples in size
Spain confirms its first wildfire death, near Madrid
Over 250,000 people evacuated across both countries combined
Spain's interior ministry says one blaze is 'beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain'
stories.background: Gironde, the wine-and-pine-forest region around Bordeaux, has burned before — a 2022 fire there was one of Europe's worst in decades. This summer's heatwave across southern Europe has left vegetation tinder-dry, and scientists say climate change is making these fires bigger and faster-moving than in the past.
stories.what_happened: French authorities ordered new evacuations of towns in Gironde, including Bordeaux suburbs Le Haillan, Eysines and Mérignac, as a wildfire that has already burned roughly 32,700 hectares (about three times the area of Paris) and destroyed 140 homes pushed toward the city. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said more than 200,000 people have now been evacuated from the Gironde and Landes regions, calling the fire 'unprecedented' because it has grown large enough to generate its own winds. Across the border, Spain confirmed its first wildfire fatality as a blaze near Madrid burned about 10,000 hectares and a neighboring fire in Ávila province consumed 13,000–15,000 hectares more.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest simultaneous firefighting operations in Western Europe in years, threatening a major city's suburbs and a globally famous wine-growing region at the same time Spain is fighting fires it says it cannot currently contain.
stories.ripple_effects: Bordeaux's wine industry faces smoke and heat damage risk to vineyards; tourism in both regions takes a hit during peak summer season; insurers face a growing bill from repeated 'unprecedented' fire seasons; and both governments will face pressure to boost firefighting budgets and cross-border resource-sharing.
stories.why_now: It's the peak of a European summer heatwave, and forecasters expect a wind shift Saturday afternoon that could push the Gironde fire even harder toward populated areas.
stories.watch_next: Whether Saturday's forecast wind shift further spreads the Gironde fire toward Bordeaux, and whether Spain manages to contain the Madrid-area blaze.

key_terms.definition: A department (administrative region) in southwestern France around Bordeaux, known for wine and pine forests, that has repeatedly seen major wildfires in recent summers.

stories.the_lesson: Wildfires don't stay confined to remote wilderness — once heat and drought intensify enough, a fire can grow large enough to threaten a major city and even generate its own weather, overwhelming a country's firefighting capacity within days.
stories.market_link: French insurers and Bordeaux-region wine producers face potential losses; renewed scrutiny for European reinsurers on climate-catastrophe exposure.

stories.title: Oman sends a delegation to Tehran to try to keep ships moving safely through the Strait of Hormuz
key_points: Omani officials arrived in Tehran Friday for direct Hormuz talks
Iran's and Oman's foreign ministers also spoke by phone
Goal: a mechanism so commercial ships can pass safely
Separately, the US and UK are planning their own Hormuz conference
stories.background: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil, and a large share of its liquefied natural gas, has to pass through — there's no easy detour. Oman sits at the strait's mouth and, unlike most Gulf states, has kept working relationships with both Iran and the West for decades, making it the natural go-between whenever Hormuz shipping is at risk.
stories.what_happened: An Omani diplomatic delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday to discuss arrangements for the safe passage of commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also spoke by phone with Oman's foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, about regional security and vessel movement through the strait and the wider Persian Gulf.
stories.why_it_matters: With the Iran war spilling into a new Red Sea front — Houthi and Saudi strikes have been trading hits on shipping and oil infrastructure all week — a disruption to Hormuz itself is the scenario energy markets fear most. This is one of the only visibly de-escalatory moves happening anywhere in the conflict right now.
stories.ripple_effects: If Iran and Oman land a workable arrangement, it could help cap further spikes in oil and gas prices even while fighting continues elsewhere in the region. If talks fail and shipping risk through Hormuz rises, insurance costs for tankers and global energy prices could jump sharply, given how much supply funnels through that single chokepoint.
stories.why_now: Shipping risk has climbed fast this week as Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis traded strikes near the Red Sea, and both Iran and Oman appear to want guardrails around Hormuz specifically, even as the broader war continues elsewhere.
stories.watch_next: Whether the US and UK's planned international conference on Hormuz materializes, and whether Iran agrees to any lasting mechanism rather than a one-off understanding.

key_terms.definition: A roughly 33-km-wide sea passage between Iran and Oman that is the only sea route out of the Persian Gulf — about a fifth of the world's oil shipments pass through it.

stories.the_lesson: Even countries actively fighting each other, or backing opposite sides of a war, usually still have a shared interest in keeping the world's most important trade chokepoints open — because closing one hurts everyone who depends on it, including the country that controls it.
stories.market_link: A credible de-escalation signal on Hormuz is one of the few things that could cap further gains in Brent crude, which has already climbed past $100 a barrel on the back of the wider Iran war.

stories.title: Trump confirms Netanyahu's White House sit-down for Tuesday — with fresh intel on Iran's nuclear program
key_points: Trump says Netanyahu travels to Washington Monday, meets him Tuesday
Netanyahu will also attend Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral
He plans to show Trump intelligence on Iran's nuclear 'recovery' efforts
First in-person Trump-Netanyahu meeting since the Iran war reignited
stories.background: Israel and the US have been coordinating closely since Iran's ceasefire collapsed and US strikes on Iran resumed this month, now stretching past 13 straight nights. A Trump-Netanyahu meeting had been discussed for weeks without a firm date, while both governments weighed how much further to push a war that has already drawn in the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
stories.what_happened: President Trump publicly confirmed that Prime Minister Netanyahu will fly to Washington on Monday and meet him at the White House on Tuesday, July 28. Netanyahu will also attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham during the trip. Israeli officials say Netanyahu intends to present Trump with fresh intelligence suggesting Iran is quietly rebuilding its nuclear and military capacity under its wartime leadership.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the first face-to-face between the two leaders since the war restarted, so it's the moment that will show how aligned — or not — Washington and Jerusalem really are on what comes next. If Trump is persuaded by the intelligence Netanyahu brings, it raises the odds of a bigger US or Israeli move against Iran's nuclear sites rather than a negotiated pause.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil traders, already nervous after Brent crude passed $100 a barrel, will be watching for any signal out of the meeting. A hawkish outcome could push energy prices higher again; a more cautious tone could support the diplomatic track Oman is separately pursuing with Iran. Gulf states, wary of being caught in the crossfire, are watching closely too.
stories.why_now: The meeting is being scheduled now because the war has ground on for weeks without a decisive outcome, and Israeli intelligence assessments about Iran's nuclear progress under its new wartime leadership are reportedly adding urgency to get Trump's read in person.
stories.watch_next: What Trump decides after Tuesday's briefing — whether it tilts the US toward another escalation or toward giving diplomacy (including Oman's parallel Hormuz talks) more room.

key_terms.definition: How close a country is to being able to build a nuclear weapon if it decided to — the thing intelligence briefings like this one try to measure.

stories.the_lesson: In a live conflict, the most consequential meetings are often not the public statements but the private intelligence handed over behind closed doors — that's usually what actually moves a leader's decision, not the photo op.
stories.market_link: Oil and defense stocks are the assets most likely to react to signals from the meeting; any hint of imminent action against Iran could push Brent crude further above its current $100+ level.

thread.previously: We reported Netanyahu was heading to the White House for his first face-to-face with Trump since the Iran war began, without a confirmed date.
thread.changed: Trump has now confirmed the exact timeline — Netanyahu arrives Monday, meets him Tuesday July 28 — and Israeli officials say he'll bring new intelligence on Iran's nuclear recovery efforts.

stories.title: US quietly empties its two biggest Gulf air bases as Iran's retaliatory strikes keep coming
key_points: Al Udeid (Qatar) and Al Dhafra (UAE) — the US military's largest Middle East hubs — have been fully evacuated of aircraft
Satellite images show the drawdown happening gradually over recent days
Comes after Iranian strikes hit Al Udeid, Al Dhafra, Ali Al Salem (Kuwait), and Fifth Fleet-linked sites in Bahrain
Iran's retaliation for the wider US-Iran war keeps spreading across the Gulf
stories.background: Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar is the forward headquarters for US Central Command — effectively the nerve center for American air power across the Middle East. Al Dhafra in the UAE hosts US and allied fighter jets and surveillance aircraft. Both became targets as Iran widened its retaliation for the war with the US and Israel, hitting American installations across the Gulf states that host US forces.
stories.what_happened: Satellite imagery reviewed by open-source analysts shows Al Udeid's aircraft count falling from 17 to just 3 before the base was completely emptied; Al Dhafra has seen a similar drawdown. The moves follow Iranian strikes on Al Udeid, Al Dhafra, Ali Al Salem in Kuwait, and Fifth Fleet-linked sites in Bahrain, as Tehran's retaliation for the US-Iran war expands to hit bases across the Gulf.
stories.why_it_matters: These two bases are the backbone of US air power in the Middle East — emptying them means either a deliberate defensive precaution against further Iranian strikes, or a signal the US is repositioning for a different phase of the conflict. Either way, it shows Washington now treats its own regional bases as under real threat, not just Israel or shipping lanes.
stories.ripple_effects: Gulf host nations (Qatar, UAE) face pressure over hosting US forces that draw Iranian fire onto their own soil. Oil markets, already jumpy over the war, watch base security as a proxy for how contained the conflict is. A prolonged US drawdown could embolden further Iranian strikes if Tehran reads it as reduced US appetite for direct confrontation.
stories.why_now: The evacuation became visible via satellite imagery in the days leading up to today, following the latest wave of Iranian drone and missile attacks on US-linked Gulf bases.
stories.watch_next: Whether the US redeploys aircraft back to the region or opens new basing elsewhere in the Gulf, or whether Iran expands strikes to bases that haven't been hit yet.

key_terms.definition: US Central Command — the part of the US military responsible for operations across the Middle East, Central Asia, and parts of South Asia.

stories.the_lesson: In modern warfare, a country's overseas military bases are as vulnerable to precision strikes as any other target — being the property of a global military power doesn't guarantee safety just because of proximity to a conflict zone.
stories.market_link: Crude oil remains elevated on fears of supply disruption; a perceived US drawdown from the region can add a fresh geopolitical risk premium to oil futures.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Iran had fired drones at US bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan as its retaliation for the war spread across the Gulf.
thread.changed: The US has now fully evacuated aircraft from its two largest regional hubs, Al Udeid (Qatar) and Al Dhafra (UAE), after strikes hit those bases too — a much bigger step than the drone attacks reported yesterday.

stories.title: US measles cases hit a 35-year high — over 2,300 confirmed as vaccine hesitancy grows
key_points: 2,318 confirmed US measles cases in 2026 — the most since 1991
93% of this year's cases are in unvaccinated people
Kindergarten vaccination rates have slipped to about 92%, below the 95% needed for herd immunity
35 separate outbreaks recorded so far, and cases are still rising
stories.background: Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 thanks to a highly effective two-dose vaccine (MMR) — meaning the disease no longer spread continuously on its own, even though travelers occasionally brought cases in. Rising vaccine hesitancy over the past several years, especially in some states and communities, has been chipping away at the immunity level that kept those imported cases from turning into bigger outbreaks.
stories.what_happened: The CDC has confirmed 2,318 measles cases across the US so far in 2026 — already above all of 2025's total (2,289 cases, itself a record) and the highest count since 1991, when 9,643 cases were recorded. Officials say 93% of this year's cases are outbreak-linked, and the same share are in people who were not vaccinated. There have been 35 distinct outbreaks so far.
stories.why_it_matters: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine — a single infected person can spread it to 9 out of 10 unvaccinated people nearby. Hitting a 35-year case high signals the US is losing the herd immunity that used to make outbreaks fizzle out quickly, raising the risk that measles becomes a constantly-circulating disease again instead of a rare imported case.
stories.ripple_effects: School vaccination requirements and exemption rules are likely to face renewed political fights in affected states. Hospitals dealing with outbreaks face higher costs for isolation wards and contact tracing. Countries with strong elimination records may start screening travelers from the US the way they currently do for countries with ongoing outbreaks.
stories.why_now: The CDC released updated year-to-date figures today showing the 35-year record has been broken — the second year in a row the US has broken its own modern-era case count.
stories.watch_next: Whether case counts keep climbing through the rest of the year, and whether any state responds by tightening school vaccine exemption rules.

key_terms.definition: When enough people in a community are immune to a disease — through vaccination or past infection — that it can't find enough new hosts to keep spreading, protecting even those who aren't immune.
The combined measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, given in two doses, that is roughly 97% effective at preventing measles.

stories.the_lesson: Disease elimination isn't a permanent state — it's maintained only as long as vaccination rates stay above a threshold (about 95% for measles). Once participation drops below that line, diseases thought long-defeated can come roaring back without any single dramatic event triggering it.

stories.title: Odds of a surprise Fed rate hike this month triple in a week, as Iran-war oil prices revive inflation fears
key_points: Markets now price roughly a 1-in-3 chance the Fed hikes rates on July 29, up from about 1-in-10 a week ago
Brent crude topping $100/barrel on Iran-war escalation is the main trigger
Fed governors Waller and Jefferson have both flagged they'd support tightening if inflation stays hot
Core inflation is running at 3.7%, well above the Fed's 2% target
stories.background: The Federal Reserve (the Fed) is the US central bank — it sets short-term interest rates to try to keep inflation (the rate prices rise) low while keeping the job market healthy. Markets constantly bet on what the Fed will do next using a tool called the CME FedWatch tool, which converts trader bets into implied probabilities. For most of this year, the Fed was expected to hold rates steady or even cut them, since a rate hike makes borrowing (mortgages, business loans, credit cards) more expensive.
stories.what_happened: The probability of a Fed interest-rate hike at the July 28-29 meeting has more than tripled over the past week, rising from about 10.7% to nearly 35-38%, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The jump followed Brent crude oil crossing $100 a barrel for the first time since May, driven by the escalating US-Iran conflict and attacks on Saudi oil facilities. Fed governor Christopher Waller said the Fed would need to 'consider tightening monetary policy in the near term' if another hot inflation reading arrives, while Governor Lisa Cook flagged core inflation already running at 3.7%, nearly double the Fed's 2% target.
stories.why_it_matters: A surprise hike would be a sharp reversal — markets had been positioned for the Fed to hold or cut, not raise rates — and would tighten financial conditions across stocks, mortgages, and corporate borrowing right as the AI-spending-fueled stock rally was already showing cracks. It's also a clear example of geopolitics (a Middle East war) directly reshaping US monetary policy.
stories.ripple_effects: Higher hike odds tend to lift the US dollar and short-term bond yields while pressuring stocks, especially rate-sensitive sectors like tech and real estate. Emerging markets including India, which import oil and borrow in dollars, face a double hit: costlier oil imports plus a stronger dollar making their own currencies weaker. Expect volatility in rate-sensitive assets through the July 29 decision.
stories.why_now: Oil's jump above $100/barrel this week is the direct trigger — energy costs feed quickly into headline inflation, which is what's forcing the Fed's hand just days before its scheduled meeting.
stories.watch_next: The FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) rate decision on July 29 at 2pm ET — and any fresh core-inflation data released before then.

key_terms.definition: Inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices — the number the Fed watches most closely as a sign of underlying price pressure.
Federal Open Market Committee — the Fed group that meets roughly every six weeks to set US interest rates.

stories.the_lesson: Central banks don't set policy in a vacuum — a war on the other side of the world that moves oil prices can flip a rate-cut expectation into a rate-hike risk within days.
stories.market_link: A hike (or even higher odds of one) pressures US equities and rate-sensitive sectors, strengthens the dollar, and adds to the case for elevated bond yields; oil-importing markets like India face added currency and inflation stress.

stories.title: Nvidia and South Korea's SK Group unveil a $500 billion-plus AI buildout — chips, memory, and data centers
key_points: Nvidia and SK Group announced letters of intent worth $500bn+ in AI infrastructure
SK Hynix will secure Nvidia's next-gen memory supply and co-develop HBM4 chips
SK Telecom to build a 2-gigawatt AI data center on Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips, live in 2027
Nvidia is also putting $1bn into Naver, and Samsung struck a related $200bn deal with Broadcom
stories.background: Building a modern AI system needs three things at once: powerful processor chips (Nvidia's specialty), the ultra-fast memory chips that feed data to those processors (called HBM, or High Bandwidth Memory — SK Hynix is a world leader here), and the physical data centers to house it all. As AI models get bigger, all three have become scarce and expensive, so the companies that make them are increasingly locking each other into long-term supply deals rather than competing openly on the spot market. South Korea's SK Group and Samsung are the two dominant global suppliers of this HBM memory.
stories.what_happened: Nvidia and South Korea's SK Group announced a more than $500 billion initiative spanning AI data centers and next-generation memory, formalized via letters of intent at an AI summit in San Francisco. SK Hynix will supply Nvidia with next-gen HBM4 memory, SK Telecom will build a 2-gigawatt AI data center powered by Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin chips (due online in 2027), and Nvidia is separately investing $1 billion in Korean cloud firm Naver. In a related move, Samsung Electronics signed an estimated $200 billion memory-and-foundry agreement with chip designer Broadcom.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest AI infrastructure commitments announced to date, and it shows the AI boom's bottleneck has shifted from chip designs to the physical supply chain — memory, power, and data-center capacity. Locking in Korean memory supply years in advance also reduces the risk that a shortage (like the one that hit HBM prices in 2024-25) could slow down Nvidia's ability to ship AI chips.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect SK Hynix and Samsung shares to react to guaranteed multi-year demand; rival memory makers like Micron may face pressure to strike similar mega-deals or lose share. For South Korea, this cements its position as indispensable to the global AI supply chain, adding leverage in trade talks with the US. It also raises the stakes on power infrastructure — a 2-gigawatt data center needs roughly the electricity of a small country, intensifying debates about grid capacity and energy costs wherever these centers are built.
stories.why_now: AI companies are racing to lock in memory and data-center capacity years ahead of need, because HBM production takes years to scale and 2027-28 AI compute demand is already being planned for today.
stories.watch_next: Watch for SK Hynix's next earnings report for detail on order volume, and for whether Micron or other memory makers announce a competing mega-deal in response.

key_terms.definition: A type of ultra-fast memory chip stacked in layers, used to feed data quickly to AI processors — a key bottleneck in building AI systems.
A formal but non-binding agreement stating two parties plan to do a deal, ahead of final contracts.

stories.the_lesson: In fast-growing industries, the real constraint often isn't the flashiest technology (the AI chip) but the unglamorous supply chain behind it (memory, power, data centers) — that's usually where the money and the risk both concentrate.
stories.market_link: Bullish for Nvidia (NVDA), SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics; watch Micron (MU) for a competitive response and any Korean-won strength on the investment inflow.

stories.title: Spain declares its first-ever national wildfire emergency as Spain and France's fire season hits a record — over 250,000 evacuated
key_points: Spain's government declared a national state of emergency for the Madrid and Ávila regions — something it has never done before for wildfires
More than 250,000 people have now fled fires across Spain and France combined
Spain has already recorded 29 major forest fires in 2026, more than triple its 10-year average of 9
About 114,800 hectares have burned in Spain this year — more than 4x last year's total at the same point
stories.background: Southern Europe has faced worsening wildfire seasons for years as summers get hotter and drier, a trend scientists tie to climate change. The current wave began with fires reaching Sicily and forcing evacuations near Bordeaux, killing three firefighters. Since then the fires have spread and intensified around Madrid.
stories.what_happened: Spain's interior ministry declared a national state of emergency for the Madrid and Ávila regions on Friday, citing simultaneous fire outbreaks and adverse weather that require pulling in resources from across the country — a first for Spain. Roughly 10,000 people were evacuated in the Madrid region alone; combined with evacuations in southern France (where 60,000+ residents fled, some by boat), more than 250,000 people have now been displaced by the fires. Spain's environment ministry says the country has already logged 29 major fires in 2026 against a decade-average of 9, with about 114,800 hectares burned versus roughly 25,100 hectares by the same point in 2025.
stories.why_it_matters: Declaring a national emergency is an unprecedented institutional step for Spain — it means the normal, region-by-region firefighting response wasn't enough, and the country has to marshal national resources instead. It's a concrete sign that this fire season is outpacing the response systems Spain already had in place.
stories.ripple_effects: France is separately requesting EU mutual-aid firefighting planes and personnel, competing for the same shared pool of resources Spain may also need. Tourism in the Madrid region is likely to take a hit during peak summer season, and insurers and reinsurers will be tallying a costlier-than-usual European fire season.
stories.why_now: The emergency declaration itself is new as of Friday (July 24) — a fresh legal and institutional escalation on top of the fire activity and evacuations already under way.
stories.watch_next: Whether the national emergency is extended to more Spanish regions, whether the EU deploys its shared RescEU firefighting fleet, and the final tally of hectares burned once the season ends.

key_terms.definition: A formal government declaration that unlocks extra powers and resources — here, letting Spain's central government mobilize firefighting help across regional lines instead of leaving each region to cope alone.

stories.the_lesson: When a disaster forces a government to invoke a power it has never used before, that's often a clearer signal of severity than the raw casualty count — institutions escalate their own response only when existing tools are visibly failing.
stories.market_link: European insurers and reinsurers face a costlier-than-usual claims season as burned-area records stack up across Spain and France.

stories.title: Netanyahu heads to the White House for his first face-to-face with Trump since the Iran war began
key_points: Netanyahu will meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday — their first in-person talks since the war on Iran started
The visit comes after two straight weeks of near-nightly US airstrikes on Iran, with no ceasefire in sight
Reports say the two leaders have quietly clashed over whether to keep bombing or seek a negotiated exit
Netanyahu will also attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Israel's closest allies in Congress
stories.background: Israel, the US and Iran have been at war since a ceasefire agreement collapsed earlier this year, and the US has since carried out over two weeks of daily airstrikes on Iranian targets. Trump and Netanyahu are longtime allies, but the two have reportedly differed privately on strategy — Trump has floated both continued strikes and a renewed push for talks, while Netanyahu has pushed to keep military pressure on Tehran. Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican and one of Israel's most vocal defenders in Washington, died on July 12 after a sudden illness; his funeral services run July 28-29.
stories.what_happened: Netanyahu's office confirmed he will fly to Washington and meet Trump at the White House on Tuesday — their first face-to-face conversation since the Iran war began. The same trip will take him to Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral. The meeting comes as the US bombing campaign against Iran approaches its two-week mark with no resolution yet.
stories.why_it_matters: A war being run by two allies who don't fully agree on strategy is inherently unstable — Netanyahu and Trump have to align on whether the goal is continued military pressure or a diplomatic off-ramp. Whatever comes out of this meeting will likely set the direction of the war for weeks to come, and it's the most direct read investors and other governments will get on whether the US plans to escalate, hold steady, or wind down.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil markets, which have been jumpy on every twist in the Iran war (crude broke past $100 a barrel this week), will react to any signal from the meeting. Gulf allies like Saudi Arabia, now drawn into their own fight with Iran-backed Houthi rebels, are watching for whether the US commits to a longer campaign or pulls back. Congress and the Israeli public will also parse the visit for signs of daylight between the two leaders.
stories.why_now: The meeting is happening now because it was scheduled around Graham's funeral — but it lands at a moment when the war has run two full weeks with mounting economic and diplomatic costs, forcing the allies to take stock of where it's headed.
stories.watch_next: Whether the two leaders publicly commit to continued strikes, announce any pause, or signal a return to negotiations after Tuesday's meeting.

key_terms.definition: A tear in the wall of the body's main artery — the sudden medical event that killed Senator Graham.

stories.the_lesson: When two allies are jointly running a war, watch for the moments their strategies might diverge — a scheduled meeting between leaders can be as important a signal for where a conflict is headed as any battlefield development.
stories.market_link: Any sign of de-escalation from the meeting could ease Brent crude prices, which just topped $100/barrel on Iran-war fears; continued-strikes signals would likely keep the war-risk premium in oil and defense stocks elevated.

stories.title: Iran rejects Trump's claim it's 'getting more serious' about talks — a general says Tehran would welcome a US ground invasion
key_points: Trump said Friday the US and Iran are still talking and Tehran is 'getting more serious'
An Iranian general publicly dismissed that, saying Iran's war is 'one that will not end'
The same general said Iran wants US ground troops to 'find themselves in a position where we can engage them'
No new US strikes were reported Friday night, after 13 consecutive nights of bombing
stories.background: The US, Israel and Iran agreed a memorandum of understanding weeks ago meant to open 60 days of talks toward a wider peace deal covering Iran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz. That truce collapsed, and the US has since bombed targets inside Iran for 13 straight nights. Trump has said he could end the war either 'diplomatically or militarily,' and has floated both continued talks and a bigger strike.
stories.what_happened: Speaking Friday, Trump said the US and Iran remain in contact and that he believes Iran is 'getting more serious' about a negotiated end to the war. An Iranian military official identified by state media as General Asadi publicly rejected that characterization, saying Iran's fight is a 'war of attrition' with no end date, and adding Iran hopes American ground forces put themselves in a position where Iran 'can engage them on the ground.' Trump separately told reporters the US military is 'locked and loaded' for a heavier attack if Iran doesn't return to serious talks.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the clearest public signal yet that the diplomatic track both sides claim to want is not actually moving — each side is describing the other's posture completely differently in public, which is usually a sign talks are stuck, not progressing. Iran inviting a ground war, even rhetorically, is a marked escalation from purely defensive language.
stories.ripple_effects: Markets read 'no ceasefire progress' as a reason to keep pricing in oil-supply risk and geopolitical uncertainty; it also raises the odds Trump orders the larger strike he has floated, which would be a bigger deal for Gulf shipping, oil prices and US domestic politics than the strikes so far.
stories.why_now: The comments were exchanged on the same day — Friday, July 24 — that a rare quiet night (no reported US strikes) raised hopes a pause might hold; both sides used the lull to stake out hard public positions instead.
stories.watch_next: Whether Trump follows through on the 'locked and loaded' threat of a bigger strike, or whether a second quiet night turns into an actual pause.

key_terms.definition: A strategy of wearing an enemy down over a long time through continuous losses, rather than winning one decisive battle.

stories.the_lesson: When two sides in a conflict both publicly claim talks are 'progressing' but describe completely different realities, that mismatch is itself the signal — real diplomatic progress usually looks like both sides going quiet, not both sides making public statements.
stories.market_link: Crude oil (Brent/WTI) and the VIX both move on escalation risk here; a confirmed pause would likely ease oil prices and risk-off sentiment across global equities.

stories.title: Houthi missiles and drones hit Saudi Aramco's Jazan and Yanbu oil sites, opening a new Red Sea front in the Iran war
key_points: Yemen's Houthi rebels say they fired 'dozens' of ballistic missiles and drones at Aramco facilities in Jazan and Yanbu overnight
Satellite fire-detection data showed active blazes and heat signatures at the Jazan complex
Comes ~24 hours after a Saudi-led coalition bombed Houthi positions in the port of Hodeidah
Houthis have vowed 'escalation with escalation' as the wider US-Iran war grinds into a third week
stories.background: Saudi Arabia has stayed mostly on the sidelines of the US-Israel-Iran war that began roughly two weeks ago, worried that taking sides could make its own oil infrastructure a target. Yemen's Houthi movement, which controls the country's northwest and is backed by Iran, has fought a Saudi-led coalition for a decade and separately declared solidarity with Iran once the US started bombing it. Aramco is the Saudi state oil company and the single biggest supplier of crude to the world market — any disruption to its refineries moves prices instantly.
stories.what_happened: Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck Aramco's Jazan refinery on the Red Sea coast and its Yanbu export terminal further north with a barrage of missiles and drones. The strikes could not be independently verified by international media, but satellite imagery analyzed by NASA's FIRMS fire-tracking system showed thermal anomalies consistent with fires at Jazan. The attack came about a day after a Saudi-led coalition struck Houthi military positions in the Yemeni port city of Hodeidah — the first time Riyadh has taken direct military action in the broader Iran conflict.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the first time Saudi Arabia's own oil infrastructure has been hit since the Iran war began, which is exactly the scenario Riyadh spent two weeks trying to avoid. It shows the conflict is spreading sideways — from a US-Iran-Israel fight into a Saudi-Houthi-Yemen fight — even as the original war shows no sign of ending.
stories.ripple_effects: Any credible threat to Saudi refining capacity pushes oil prices higher worldwide, which raises fuel and shipping costs everywhere, including in India, which imports most of its crude. It also raises the odds that Saudi Arabia gets pulled deeper into the war it was trying to sit out, and it could complicate the already-stalled US-Iran ceasefire talks, since Iran-backed Houthi actions now sit alongside direct US-Iran strikes on the negotiating table.
stories.why_now: The Houthis explicitly linked this strike to the Saudi-led coalition's attack on Hodeidah a day earlier, framing it as retaliation — 'escalation with escalation,' in their words.
stories.watch_next: Watch Aramco's own statement (or silence) on Jazan and Yanbu output, and whether Brent crude extends its move toward $100/barrel on the news.

key_terms.definition: An armed movement, backed by Iran, that controls most of northern Yemen and has fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015.
Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company — the world's largest oil producer by output, and central to global crude supply.

stories.the_lesson: In a war between two countries, watch the countries that didn't want to be involved — their infrastructure is often what actually moves the oil price, because attacking a bystander's supply is 'safer' for the aggressor than attacking the main combatant.
stories.market_link: Brent and WTI crude, Indian oil-marketing companies (IOC, BPCL, HPCL), and the rupee (a weaker rupee and pricier oil both squeeze India's import bill) are the direct channels; sustained Saudi supply risk also lifts defense and shipping-insurance names.

stories.title: Paramount agrees to delay its Warner Bros. Discovery buyout until mid-2027 as state lawsuits threaten to kill the deal
key_points: Paramount won't close the Warner Bros. Discovery deal until a court rules on an antitrust challenge, or June 1, 2027 — whichever comes first
A federal judge had already ordered a 2-week halt to the merger earlier in the week
12 state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, are suing to block it outright
The Writers Guild of America filed a separate suit, saying the merger would mean lower pay and fewer jobs for writers
stories.background: Paramount (owner of CBS and Paramount Pictures) agreed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery (owner of HBO, CNN, and Warner Bros. studios) in one of the largest media mergers in Hollywood history — combining two major studios, two streaming services, and a stack of TV networks into one company. Big mergers like this need antitrust approval because regulators worry about one company controlling too much of an industry, which can mean higher prices and fewer choices for consumers.
stories.what_happened: Paramount said in a Friday afternoon court filing that it will not complete the merger until either an antitrust trial takes place or June 1, 2027, whichever is sooner. This came just days after a federal judge had already ordered the two companies to pause the deal for at least two weeks while a legal challenge from a coalition of state attorneys general plays out. The Writers Guild of America filed its own separate lawsuit making similar antitrust arguments.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a real threat to one of the biggest media deals in years, not just a paperwork delay. If the states win, the merger could be blocked entirely, reshaping who controls Hollywood's studios and streaming services. Every quarter the deal is delayed, Paramount also owes Warner Bros. Discovery a contractual 'ticking fee' — extra money that makes waiting expensive for Paramount.
stories.ripple_effects: A prolonged delay adds real cost pressure on Paramount and creates uncertainty for both companies' employees, especially writers and other creative workers the WGA says would be hurt by less competition among studios. It also sets a precedent other media and tech mergers will watch closely — state attorneys general successfully forcing a pause signals they're willing to fight big consolidation deals even after federal regulators have weighed in.
stories.why_now: The delay was forced by a fast-moving legal fight: a federal judge ordered a halt earlier in the week, and state AGs plus the WGA filed suits within days of each other in mid-July, escalating pressure that led Paramount to concede the delay rather than fight to close on the original schedule.
stories.watch_next: The antitrust trial date and any ruling on the states' request for an injunction — that outcome decides whether the merger proceeds at all.

key_terms.definition: A legal case arguing that a merger or business practice illegally reduces competition, which can lead to higher prices or fewer choices for consumers.
A penalty payment, often per share per quarter, that one company owes another for delaying a deal's closing — it makes stalling costly.

stories.the_lesson: Even after two companies and their boards agree to merge, government lawyers — federal or state — can still delay or kill the deal if they believe it hurts competition. Regulatory risk doesn't end at the handshake; it can drag on for years and cost real money.
stories.market_link: Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery shares are sensitive to every twist in this case; a prolonged delay or a block would hit merger-arbitrage investors betting on the deal closing on schedule.

stories.title: Trump rolls out new 10–12.5% tariffs on 60 countries over 'forced labor' — the replacement for the tariffs the Supreme Court struck down
key_points: New tariffs of 10% or 12.5% now apply to goods from 60 countries, covering over 99% of all US imports
Legal basis this time is a forced-labor law (Section 301), not the emergency powers law the Supreme Court rejected in February
Countries get the lower 10% rate if they've banned forced-labor imports, 12.5% if they haven't
Trade partners are furious and legal challenges have already been filed
stories.background: In February 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that Trump's original 'Liberation Day' tariffs were illegal — the emergency-powers law he used (called IEEPA) doesn't actually let a president impose tariffs, the Court said. That should have ended the blanket tariffs. Instead, the administration spent months building a legal workaround: investigations into whether America's 60 biggest trading partners were doing enough to stop goods made with forced labor from entering their supply chains.
stories.what_happened: Those new tariffs took effect on July 24, 2026. They use a different law — Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which lets a president retaliate against 'unfair trade practices' — instead of the law the Supreme Court struck down. US trade investigators concluded all 60 partners had failed to adequately block forced-labor goods, triggering duties of 10% (for countries that have at least banned such imports on paper) or 12.5% (for those that haven't). Together the 60 countries account for 99.4% of US trade.
stories.why_it_matters: This is Trump effectively rebuilding the same broad tariff wall the Supreme Court just tore down, using a different legal doorway. If it holds up, it resets import costs across nearly all of US trade — the exact outcome the Court's ruling was supposed to prevent. If it doesn't hold up in court, it's another few months of tariff whiplash for businesses trying to plan.
stories.ripple_effects: Companies that import goods — retailers, manufacturers, electronics firms — face higher costs again just as they'd adjusted to the tariffs being voided, likely passing some of it on to consumers. Trading partners, who see the 'forced labor' justification as a pretext, are weighing retaliation, which could reignite trade fights with the EU, China, and others. Legal challenges are already filed, so this could head back toward the Supreme Court.
stories.why_now: The administration moved fast to have a replacement ready the moment the old tariffs were struck down, rather than let the country go tariff-free even briefly — and July 24 was when the USTR's forced-labor investigations formally concluded.
stories.watch_next: Watch the first court rulings on the new lawsuits — a fast injunction would signal this workaround is as legally shaky as the last one.

key_terms.definition: The International Emergency Economic Powers Act — a law letting presidents act during declared emergencies. The Supreme Court ruled it doesn't cover imposing tariffs.
A different, older trade law that lets a president impose tariffs specifically to retaliate against 'unfair' foreign trade practices — the legal route used this time.

stories.the_lesson: When a court strikes down a policy on narrow legal grounds, that often isn't the end — governments frequently just find a different legal lever to reach the same goal. Watch the substance of a policy, not just which law it's parked under.
stories.market_link: Broad tariff resets like this move currency and equity markets tied to US trade exposure — export-heavy sectors and countries on the 12.5% list are most at risk of margin pressure.

thread.previously: Yesterday's story reported that Trump's original blanket 10% tariff was expiring by law and that a replacement was already being prepared.
thread.changed: That replacement is now live: a 60-country, forced-labor-justified tariff regime took effect July 24, using a different law than the one the Supreme Court struck down.

stories.title: Wall Street's 'Magnificent Seven' shed $797 billion in a day on AI-spending fears — then claw back some ground as a volatile week closes
key_points: The 'Magnificent Seven' megacap tech index fell 4.8% Thursday, its worst one-day drop since April 2025's tariff shock
Tesla plunged nearly 15%, Alphabet fell more than 7%, wiping out $797 billion in combined market value
Trigger: investor worry that Big Tech's ballooning AI spending has an unclear payoff, compounded by the Iran war clouding the macro outlook
Friday: Nasdaq slipped further but the Dow and S&P 500 recovered, closing a rocky week roughly flat
stories.background: The 'Magnificent Seven' — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta and Tesla — have driven most of the US stock market's gains since 2023, largely on excitement about AI. Those same seven companies have also been ploughing hundreds of billions of dollars a year into AI data centers and chips. For most of that run, investors rewarded the spending; lately, they've started asking when — or whether — it turns into profit.
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, the Magnificent Seven index fell 4.8%, erasing $797 billion in value in a single session as investors reacted to fresh disclosures of surging AI capital expenditure from the group, layered on top of oil near $100 a barrel and war-driven risk aversion. Tesla dropped nearly 15% despite reporting record revenue; Alphabet fell over 7%. The S&P 500 fell 1.2% and the Nasdaq 100 sank 1.9% that day. By Friday's close, the Nasdaq Composite dipped a further 0.64% but the Dow gained 0.46% and the S&P 500 was roughly flat, as the week ended without a full-blown rout.
stories.why_it_matters: Because these seven stocks make up an outsized share of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, their swings move retirement accounts and index funds well beyond anyone who consciously 'bet on AI.' The selloff is a real-time test of whether investors still believe the AI buildout will pay for itself.
stories.ripple_effects: Asian chip suppliers like Samsung and SK Hynix had already wobbled earlier this month on the same worry. A sustained pullback in AI capex plans would ripple into chipmakers, data-center builders, and power utilities that had been pricing in years of AI-driven demand growth. It also raises the stakes for the next round of hyperscaler earnings.
stories.why_now: This week's earnings disclosures forced Big Tech to spell out just how much it's spending on AI, right as Iran-war jitters were already pushing investors toward caution — the two pressures hit at the same time.
stories.watch_next: The next wave of hyperscaler earnings and their AI capex guidance, plus whether the Fed's tone shifts if the selloff resumes.

key_terms.definition: A nickname for the seven US megacap tech stocks — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta and Tesla — whose combined size and gains have dominated the stock market since 2023.
Money a company spends on long-term assets like buildings, chips or data centers, as opposed to day-to-day running costs — it shows up as an investment now with returns expected later, if at all.

stories.the_lesson: When a handful of mega-cap stocks make up an outsized share of the index, a shift in sentiment on just one theme — like AI spending — can move the whole market, not just the sector it's about.
stories.market_link: Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 futures, plus AI-linked chipmakers (Nvidia, AMD) and Asian suppliers (Samsung, SK Hynix), are the names most sensitive to any further wobble in the AI trade.

stories.title: Trump says a 'massive attack' on Iran 'may not be necessary,' floats negotiations as US strikes hit a 13th straight night
key_points: Trump: the massive strike he threatened a day earlier 'may not be necessary'
Says Iran wants a deal but 'isn't ready' to sign one yet
US bombing campaign continued into a 13th consecutive night
Some Gulf allies reportedly losing patience with the daily escalation
stories.background: The US-Iran war reignited weeks ago after a fragile ceasefire collapsed, and Washington has since carried out nightly strikes on Iranian military and nuclear-linked sites while Iran has hit back at US bases and shipping across the Gulf and Red Sea. On Thursday, Trump said he was 'considering a massive attack, bigger than ever before' and 'close to making a decision,' telling Iran it 'hasn't received enough pain yet.' The US House had already voted a second time, in a rare bipartisan rebuke, to try to end Trump's war powers over the conflict.
stories.what_happened: A day after threatening an unprecedented 'massive attack,' Trump told reporters on Friday afternoon that it 'may not be necessary,' saying Iran wants to negotiate but isn't yet ready to make a deal. Even as he left the door open to talks, US strikes on Iran continued for a 13th straight night, and Iran kept up retaliatory attacks on US-linked targets in the Gulf.
stories.why_it_matters: The shift in tone — from an explicit escalation threat to 'may not be necessary' — is the clearest signal yet that Washington may be looking for an exit ramp, even as the bombing continues on the ground. For a region already on edge, the gap between Trump's words and the military's actions is itself a source of instability.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil markets, which have been trading near $100 a barrel on war risk, react quickly to any hint of de-escalation or its opposite. Gulf allies hosting US forces are exposed to Iranian retaliation with every night the strikes continue, and reporting suggests some are growing impatient. In Washington, the mixed signals fuel the bipartisan Congressional effort to claw back war-powers authority from the White House.
stories.why_now: Thirteen consecutive nights of strikes is a heavy operational and diplomatic burden, and Trump faces an actual decision point on whether to escalate further — the 'may not be necessary' comment reads as him keeping that option open while testing whether pressure alone gets Iran to the table.
stories.watch_next: Whether Trump follows through on the threatened 'massive attack' in the coming days, or whether backchannel talks (Pakistan has reportedly been trying to broker a restart) produce a real ceasefire framework.

key_terms.definition: The US Constitution splits military authority between Congress (which can declare war) and the President (commander-in-chief) — Congress can vote to limit a president's ability to keep US forces in a conflict without its approval.

stories.the_lesson: Threatening a bigger escalation while simultaneously saying it 'may not be necessary' is a classic pressure tactic — it keeps every option open and forces the other side to guess, without the threatening party having to commit to anything yet.
stories.market_link: Oil prices and Gulf-exposed shipping and insurance stocks remain highly sensitive to any signal of imminent US escalation or de-escalation with Iran.

thread.changed: By Friday afternoon, Trump softened that to the massive attack 'may not be necessary,' saying Iran wants to negotiate — even as US strikes continued for a 13th straight night and Gulf allies show signs of losing patience.
